meta.title: Nadia's Pool Rules
meta.textType: functional: an email with safety rules

paragraphs: On Saturday, November seventh, Mia sat at her desk and opened a new email. It came from her pen pal Nadia. Snow, her white kitten, sat next to the laptop. The subject of the email was "Pool Rules." Mia read the first lines out loud. "Dear Mia, this week I want to tell you about the rules of my swimming pool." "Swimming is good exercise, but we must be careful." "Please read the rules, and remember them."

"Here are six rules." "One: shower before you swim." "Two: do not run or hurry on the wet floor." "Three: do not jump into the shallow end, because the water is not deep." "Four: children under twelve cannot swim without an adult, except in the small pool." "Five: you don't have to wear a cap, but you must tie long hair." "Six: be polite to the lifeguard, and follow the lifeguard's words." "A sign at the deep end says, Danger: Deep Water."

"Beginners stay in the shallow end, and the lifeguard watches everybody." "Does your town pool have rules, too?" "Best wishes, Nadia." "P.S. Please say hello to Snow and Pip." Mia smiled at the last line. Then she took her notebook and got ready to write. She drew a pool with a deep end and a shallow end. Under the drawing she wrote, "Questions for Nadia." Her first question was, "What do the signs at your pool look like?" Her second question was, "Which rule is the most important for you?"

Mia read rule four again. "I am eleven, so I cannot swim without an adult," she said to Snow. "But I can swim with my mom, and I always remember to shower first." "I think the town pool has rules, too." Snow jumped up on the desk and sat on the notebook. Mia laughed and moved her.

Then Mia typed her answer. "Dear Nadia, thank you for your pool rules." "I like rule four, because it keeps children safe." "Tomorrow I will take photos of the signs at our town pool." "Then I will send them to you." "Best wishes, Mia." "P.S. Snow says hello, and I will tell Pip, too." Mia sent the email and smiled.
